publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Evidence that the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is rapidly accumulating plastic

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how much buoyant plastic is floating in the North Pacific accumulation zone, of what sizes and types, and whether the amount is changing
span.quote: We predicted that the GPGP contains a total of 1.8 (mid-point estimate, low: 1.1, high: 3.6) trillion plastic pieces weighing 79 k (45 k−129 k) tonnes, comprised of debris categorised in 4 size classes: microplastics (0.05–0.5 cm), mesoplastics (0.5–5 cm), macroplastics (5–50 cm), and megaplastics (>50 cm).

span.label: whether the mass of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch has been underestimated because the instruments used to measure it cannot catch its largest and rarest debris
span.quote: Most available data on quantities and characteristics of buoyant ocean plastic are derived from samples collected with small sea surface trawls initially developed to collect neustonic plankton. Due to their small aperture (0.5–1 m width, 0.15–1 m depth) and limited surface area covered, they could underestimate loads of rarer and larger plastic objects such as bottles, buoys and fishing nets.

span.label: 79 (45-129) thousand tonnes and 1.8 (1.1-3.6) trillion pieces over 1.6 million km2, from 652 net tows plus 311 km2 of aerial imagery calibrated into a time-resolved transport model - four to sixteen times previous estimates, with the method difference and the rival explanation both named
span.quote: Our plastic mass estimate for the GPGP (~79 k tonnes) was nearly sixteen times higher than a previous study (~4.8 k tonnes) that used net trawl data only and four times higher than another assessment (~21 k tonnes) that combined net trawl data with vessel-based visual surveys. We suggest that the increase in the estimate is mainly explained by the use of more robust methods for quantifying macro- and megaplastics over larger sea surface areas. For instance, aerial imagery allowed us to more accurately count and measure the size of sighted objects, which undeniably reduced uncertainties in mass estimates when compared to vessel-based visual surveys.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We predicted that the GPGP contains a total of 1.8 (mid-point estimate, low: 1.1, high: 3.6) trillion plastic pieces weighing 79 k (45 k−129 k) tonnes, comprised of debris categorised in 4 size classes: microplastics (0.05–0.5 cm), mesoplastics (0.5–5 cm), macroplastics (5–50 cm), and megaplastics (>50 cm).

span.label: accumulation of buoyant plastic in a subtropical gyre, dominated by mass in objects large enough that a plankton net was never going to see them
span.quote: More than three quarters of the GPGP plastic mass was contained in the upper size classes (>5 cm), with a respective total contribution of 25% and 53% for macroplastics and megaplastics (Fig. 4a). Plastic types ‘H’ (hard plastics, sheets and films) and ‘N’ (nets, ropes and lines) represented respectively 47% and 52% of the total GPGP plastic mass, with most of micro-, meso- and macroplastic mass coming from type ‘H’, and megaplastic from type ‘N’. Two additional plastic types, pellets (type ‘P’) and foams (type ‘F’) were also observed in a few size classes, but their overall contribution to the GPGP plastic load was minimal. For megaplastics, we could also assess the mass contributions of different object types. We estimated that 86% of their 42 k tonnes contribution was carried by fishing nets.

span.label: 652 Manta and Mega net tows from 18 vessels, 7,298 georeferenced aerial mosaics, depth-integrated concentration corrections, and a Lagrangian transport model calibrated on ENSO/PDO-matched years rather than on a flat multi-year average
span.term: 652 Manta and Mega net tows from 18 vessels, 7,298 georeferenced aerial mosaics, depth-integrated concentration corrections, and a Lagrangian transport model calibrated on ENSO/PDO-matched years rather than on a flat multi-year average
span.quote: From July 27th to September 19th 2015, a total of 652 surface net tows were carried out between 25°N–41°N and 129–156°W by 18 participating vessels. In October 2016, we revisited our study area by conducting two flights with a Hercules C-130 aircraft that collected aerial imagery (n = 7,298 single-frame mosaics) to better quantify the larger and rarer >50 cm plastic objects (Fig. 1).

span.label: the standard instrument is a 90 cm net developed for plankton, covering 0.008 km2 per tow; rare metre-scale objects carry most of the mass and are almost never inside such a sample, so the measured mass is a function of how much sea surface the instrument sees rather than of how much plastic is there
span.quote: Most available data on quantities and characteristics of buoyant ocean plastic are derived from samples collected with small sea surface trawls initially developed to collect neustonic plankton. Due to their small aperture (0.5–1 m width, 0.15–1 m depth) and limited surface area covered, they could underestimate loads of rarer and larger plastic objects such as bottles, buoys and fishing nets.

span.label: films are about 37% of PE and PP waste and are rarely found here; the paper's hypothesis is that thin objects foul, sink or fragment quickly, so the patch contains not the plastic that enters the ocean but the subset able to stay at the surface
span.term: volume-to-surface ratio as a survival filter
span.quote: Firstly, the vast majority of the collected GPGP objects were made of PE and PP rigid plastics and bundled fishing nets and ropes. Plastic films however, representing around 37% of PE and PP waste generation, were rarely found. We hypothesize that most buoyant plastic with insufficient volume-to-surface ratios such as films may never reach the surface waters of the GPGP as they may rapidly sink to the seafloor due to biofouling and/or fragment into microscopic pieces that are removed from surface layers.

span.label: particles displaced by a fraction of wind speed take wider orbits, are more likely to strand and more likely to leave the gyre; low-windage objects stay - which is why the best-fitting model has no wind term and why foam is abundant on Alaskan beaches and negligible in the patch
span.term: windage sorting the debris by where it ends up
span.quote: Finally, it seems that most plastics accumulating in the GPGP region are hardly transported by winds. Our model predicted that the GPGP is dominated by objects with low or null windage coefficient, and it was the null windage forcing scenario that best represented the GPGP plastic concentrations gradients measured in this study. Furthermore, most objects captured in our trawls (e.g. broken fragments of hard plastic objects, nets and ropes) exhibited no or very little air draft when placed in seawater, and many objects sighted during the aerial expedition seemed fully submerged. Ghostnets, which were the main contributors to the total mass of GPGP plastic, generally have a draft of several metres, and therefore are unlikely to be influenced by wind transport.

span.label: the patch's centre oscillates seasonally in longitude and inter-annually in latitude with ENSO and PDO, so calibrating measurements from one season against a flat multi-year average compares them with a smear rather than with a position - matching the climate indices of the sampling year improved the fit from 0.46 to 0.58
span.term: a moving target averaged into blur
span.quote: The relation between the accumulation of marine debris in the North Pacific and climate events such as El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) has previously been discussed. As such, to account for inter-annual variation, we compared latitudinal and longitudinal position of the GPGP against these two climate indexes: ENSO and PDO. We found that 2002 and 2004 were similar to the conditions experienced during our multi-vessel expedition. Thus, we compared our measurements against particle visit averages for July–September of 2002 and 2004 combined. This second attempt exhibited better results (R2 = 0.58 to 0.41, depending on forcing scenario), suggesting that climatic events such as ENSO or PDO influence the average position of the GPGP. Therefore, we decided to use the July–September average for 2002 and 2004, which better accounts for inter-annual variations in the GPGP position.

span.label: the four-to-sixteen-fold increase over previous estimates could also be a real increase in pollution rather than a method difference, and the paper says so
span.quote: Nonetheless, differences between estimates could also be attributed to increasing levels of ocean plastic pollution in the area, and particularly plastic inputs from the 2011 Tohoku tsunami. An estimated 4.5 million tonnes of debris were washed at sea instantly, of which 70% may have sunk rapidly according to Japanese Government. This leaves 1.4 million tonnes of debris that could have been transported at the sea surface over longer distances.

span.label: the model predicts millions of tonnes in the region from accepted inputs while the surveys found tens of thousands - a two-orders-of-magnitude gap left open
span.quote: Despite an increase in the GPGP mass estimate, a great discrepancy between predicted and observed ocean plastic concentrations remains. Considering currently accepted plastic inputs from land- and marine-based sources, our global model predicted millions of tonnes of ocean plastic to be within the GPGP region, while we only found tens of thousands of tonnes. This two-orders of magnitude difference suggests the existence of mechanisms removing most of the plastic mass from the sea surface and/or fragmenting the plastic into pieces smaller than those quantified here (<0.5 mm).

span.label: the aerial survey deliberately trades false positives for false negatives: observers logged only what they were very confident about, so many possible debris features were never recorded
span.quote: We trust we had a very small number of false positives and a high number of false negatives. This is because the observers took a conservative approach: they only logged features as debris when they were very confident with its identification. As such, many features that could be debris, but resembled other natural features, such as sun glint and breaking wave, were not logged into our ocean plastic dataset.

span.label: the mass estimates are conservative by construction - sampling concentrated inside the boundary, and the outer patch is modelled at over 100k tonnes
span.quote: It is important to highlight here that our mass estimates are conservative. Most of our sampling effort were conducted inside the GPGP boundary line defined in this study. Although concentrations decreased by orders of magnitude as we moved away from the GPGP centre, when considering the outer GPGP (0.1 kg km−2 microplastic contour level, shown in Fig. 3), our model predicted over 100k tonnes of ocean plastics.

span.label: high-windage debris passing through the patch over longer periods is underestimated, because a monthly average spreads it over a larger area
span.quote: Moreover, we improved our knowledge on the quantity of plastic contained inside the GPGP over a brief period of time, but we underestimated amounts of higher windage debris that may be passing through the GPGP, while circulating the North Pacific with the subtropical gyre currents. On a monthly average, the concentration of high windage debris within the GPGP may be minimal as it is spread over a larger area than low windage debris. However, when considering debris that passes through the GPGP over a longer period of time, the contribution of high windage debris may be more substantial.

span.label: both trawls were towed at an angle so the sampled width is likely smaller than the net width used in the area calculation, and vessel wake probably affected capture
span.quote: Furthermore, some sample biases also made our estimates conservative. Regarding trawl sampling, vessel wake effects were minimized as much as possible, but it is likely that vessel-induced disturbance of the water flow affected the capture efficiency of our nets. Also, both trawls were towed at an angle (so the net moved away from vessel), which means that the width of the sampled area is likely smaller than the net width dimensions used in our area estimations.

span.label: debris may have broken during transport to the laboratory, biasing the size distribution
span.quote: Even though we were careful when handling samples, some debris items may have been broken during transportation, leading to some bias in our debris size distribution.

span.label: the degradation rate of synthetic polymers at sea is poorly understood, so how long the standing mass will persist cannot be estimated
span.quote: The degradation rate of synthetic polymers in the marine environment is poorly understood, but it is known to depend on local environmental conditions, polymer types, shape and coating of objects. The relatively high occurrence of macroplastics with production dates from the 70 s, 80 s, and 90 s compared to more recent debris suggest that specific types of plastic (i.e. with high volume-to-surface ratios and low windage) persist and accumulate in the GPGP region.

span.label: plastic levels in the deep water and seafloor below the patch are unknown, so the inventory is of one layer only
span.quote: Levels of plastic pollution in deep water layers and seafloor below the GPGP remain unknown, and could be quantified through sampling. We encourage more sampling throughout the world’s oceans, as well as the systematic monitoring of the GPGP as it is one of the few marine regions with a relatively good historical dataset that allows us to understand long-term trends in oceanic plastic pollution.

span.label: the 28.1% marine-source share is taken from coastal clean-up data and observations at sea may imply much higher losses, so the source attribution may be wrong in either direction
span.quote: Nonetheless, the GPGP dominance of marine-sourced plastics could also be attributed to their purposely engineered durability in the marine environment (e.g. strong and thick-walled nets, traps, ropes, and floats used by marine industries) as well as overestimations of land-based sources and/or underestimations of marine-based sources. In this study, we considered fishing, aquaculture and shipping to be responsible for 28.1% of the global plastic inputs into the oceans, based on coastal clean-up data; however, observations at sea may lead to much higher estimates of plastic loads being lost or discarded at sea.

span.label: Lagrangian particle advection with wave, wind and current forcing, carried from physical oceanography into an inventory of manufactured debris
span.quote: As buoyant plastics can be missed by surface trawls due to wind-driven mixing, we then estimated the ‘depth-integrated’ mass and numerical plastic concentrations (Ci) for all type/size categories at each of the trawl sampling locations using the equations described in ref.. Supplementary Methods 1 provides details on how Ci was calculated as a function of ocean plastic terminal rising velocity (Wb), depth sampled by the trawl, and sea state. It also describes how we measured Wb for each of the type/size categories of this study.

span.label: a dated, located mass release - the 2011 Tohoku tsunami - used as a natural tracer experiment to constrain a transport parameter
span.quote: The dependence of the particle trajectory on the windage coefficient predicted by our model is in good agreement with sightings and modelling of debris originated from the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan. The first identified Japanese debris items that arrived after 10 to 12 months on the North American shores were objects with high windage such as buoys, boats and floating docks. Debris also arrived on Hawaiian Islands 18 months after the incident. The time of arrival was closely related to object types, starting in the first year with large oyster farm buoys and other floats, containers, and canisters. In the second year more buoys, tipped boats, fridges, and pallets arrived, followed later by timber beams and wooden debris. Our model predicted that only objects with a windage coefficient above 3% could arrive on Hawaii in the second year after the 2011 tsunami.

span.label: two Manta and two large Neuston trawls towed simultaneously at the same 76 stations, and the paired results used to decide which device quantifies which size band
span.note: eliminates: net aperture as the source of the reported size distribution - a single device cannot tell whether the sizes it misses are absent or merely uncaught · outcome: held
span.quote: After comparing plastic concentration results obtained by paired Manta and Mega net tows (n = 76 locations), we decided to use Manta and Mega trawl samples to quantify debris 0.05–5 cm and 5–50 cm in size, respectively. The comparison results and reasoning behind such decision in provided in Supplementary Methods 2.

span.label: 311 km2 surveyed from the air against 3.9 and 13.6 km2 by Manta and Mega tow, for the size class whose rarity is the whole problem
span.note: eliminates: rarity being mistaken for absence - at trawl coverage a >50 cm object is a sampling accident, and the mass it carries cannot be estimated from its absence · outcome: held
span.quote: The aerial surveys sampled a far greater area (311.0 km2) than the trawl surveys described above (3.9 km2 and 13.6 km2, for Manta and Mega net tows, respectively), thus yielding a more reliable quantification of debris larger than 50 cm, which are relatively rare.

span.label: an experimental detection algorithm run over all 7,298 mosaics after the human pass, with every algorithm hit re-inspected by an observer before entering the database
span.note: eliminates: observer oversight as the only check on the imagery, without letting the algorithm introduce false positives of its own · outcome: partial
span.quote: Once this work was finalised, we ran an experimental algorithm capable of detecting potential debris in all our RGB mosaics as a quality control step. To avoid any false positives, all features detected by the algorithm were also visually inspected by an observer and only those visually identified as debris were logged in our QGIS database.

span.label: six forcing scenarios - current only, and 0.1 to 3% windage - each fitted against the same 277 cells of measured microplastic concentration
span.note: eliminates: the chosen transport physics being assumed rather than selected; the regression coefficient falls monotonically as wind forcing is added, so the data picks · outcome: held
span.quote: The best model fit was found for the forcing scenario with sea-surface current only (R2 = 0.52, n = 277 cells). The regression coefficient declined as we increased the atmospheric drag term (R2 = 0.39 to 0.21 depending on windage coefficient).

span.label: three calibration windows tried in sequence - a flat 12-year average, a season-matched average, and an ENSO/PDO-matched pair of years - with the fit reported for each
span.note: eliminates: an averaging window flattering the fit - the season-matched version was WORSE than the flat average and is reported as such before the better one is adopted · outcome: held
span.quote: We first decided to test our model for seasonal variation by comparing our microplastic concentrations (measured in July – September 2015) against modelled concentrations averages for the July–September periods of 2000 to 2012. This comparison yielded poorer results (R2 = 0.46 to 0.21, depending on forcing scenario) than with the 12 years average solution (R2 = 0.52) as the July–September GPGP position varied substantially among years.

span.label: measured microplastic concentrations sorted by whether they fell inside or outside the modelled 1 kg km-2 contour, as a test of the boundary the model drew
span.note: eliminates: a boundary drawn to fit the story - the contrast is measured, 1.8 against 0.3 kg km-2 in the medians, rather than asserted from the map · outcome: held
span.quote: As a validation, we categorized microplastics measurements inside and outside the 1 kg km−2 contour line (Fig. 2b). For stations inside the model-predicted GPGP, the median measured microplastic concentration was 1.8 kg km−2 (25th–75th percentiles = 3.5–0.9 kg km−2) while for stations outside, the median was 0.3 kg km−2 (25th–75th percentiles = 0.2–0.7 kg km−2).

span.label: the model's windage behaviour checked against the recorded arrival times and object types of 2011 Tohoku tsunami debris on North American and Hawaiian shores
span.note: eliminates: the windage parameterisation being unconstrained by any real trajectory - the tsunami provides a dated release of known objects that the model must reproduce · outcome: held
span.quote: The dependence of the particle trajectory on the windage coefficient predicted by our model is in good agreement with sightings and modelling of debris originated from the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan. The first identified Japanese debris items that arrived after 10 to 12 months on the North American shores were objects with high windage such as buoys, boats and floating docks. Debris also arrived on Hawaiian Islands 18 months after the incident. The time of arrival was closely related to object types, starting in the first year with large oyster farm buoys and other floats, containers, and canisters. In the second year more buoys, tipped boats, fridges, and pallets arrived, followed later by timber beams and wooden debris. Our model predicted that only objects with a windage coefficient above 3% could arrive on Hawaii in the second year after the 2011 tsunami.

span.label: exponential, linear, quadratic and cubic fits to the decadal concentration averages, with the coefficient of determination given for all four
span.note: eliminates: the exponential being chosen because it makes the stronger claim - the three alternatives are fitted and their worse fits reported · outcome: held
span.quote: Finally, we extracted decadal trends by fitting an exponential function (R2 = 0.94) assuming null concentrations at the beginning of the 20th century. The exponential fit exhibited better results than linear, quadratic or cubic functions (R2 = 0.71, R2 = 0.86 and R2 = 0.91, respectively).

span.label: historical net tows sorted into inside-boundary, outside-but-subtropical, and rest-of-North-Pacific, with the third category excluded from the comparison
span.note: eliminates: equatorial and polar samples deflating the around-the-patch baseline and manufacturing a contrast between inside and outside · outcome: held
span.quote: Using our dynamic GPGP model boundary as reference, we classified each net tow into 3 categories: (1) sampled within the GPGP boundary, (2) sampled outside the GPGP boundary, but above 20°N and below 45°N and (3) sampled in the rest of the North Pacific. We only used net tows from the first two categories above so that concentration statistics for outside the patch were not biased by measurements taken in equatorial and polar waters, where concentrations were very low.

span.label: depth-integrated concentrations computed for every trawl station as a function of rising velocity, trawl depth and sea state, to correct for wind-driven mixing
span.note: eliminates: buoyant plastic missed by a surface trawl because wind-driven mixing pushed it below the net · outcome: held
span.quote: As buoyant plastics can be missed by surface trawls due to wind-driven mixing, we then estimated the ‘depth-integrated’ mass and numerical plastic concentrations (Ci) for all type/size categories at each of the trawl sampling locations using the equations described in ref.. Supplementary Methods 1 provides details on how Ci was calculated as a function of ocean plastic terminal rising velocity (Wb), depth sampled by the trawl, and sea state. It also describes how we measured Wb for each of the type/size categories of this study.

span.label: all trawls designed to move away from the vessel so that wake would not affect capture efficiency
span.note: eliminates: vessel wake disturbing the water the net samples - the trawls were angled away to reduce it, and the paper says the effect remained · outcome: partial
span.quote: Furthermore, some sample biases also made our estimates conservative. Regarding trawl sampling, vessel wake effects were minimized as much as possible, but it is likely that vessel-induced disturbance of the water flow affected the capture efficiency of our nets. Also, both trawls were towed at an angle (so the net moved away from vessel), which means that the width of the sampled area is likely smaller than the net width dimensions used in our area estimations.

span.label: GPGP
span.quote: We predicted that the GPGP contains a total of 1.8 (mid-point estimate, low: 1.1, high: 3.6) trillion plastic pieces weighing 79 k (45 k−129 k) tonnes, comprised of debris categorised in 4 size classes: microplastics (0.05–0.5 cm), mesoplastics (0.5–5 cm), macroplastics (5–50 cm), and megaplastics (>50 cm).

span.label: microplastics
span.quote: Over three-quarters of the GPGP mass was carried by debris larger than 5 cm and at least 46% was comprised of fishing nets. Microplastics accounted for 8% of the total mass but 94% of the estimated 1.8 (1.1–3.6) trillion pieces floating in the area.

span.label: megaplastics
span.quote: More than three quarters of the GPGP plastic mass was contained in the upper size classes (>5 cm), with a respective total contribution of 25% and 53% for macroplastics and megaplastics (Fig. 4a). Plastic types ‘H’ (hard plastics, sheets and films) and ‘N’ (nets, ropes and lines) represented respectively 47% and 52% of the total GPGP plastic mass, with most of micro-, meso- and macroplastic mass coming from type ‘H’, and megaplastic from type ‘N’. Two additional plastic types, pellets (type ‘P’) and foams (type ‘F’) were also observed in a few size classes, but their overall contribution to the GPGP plastic load was minimal. For megaplastics, we could also assess the mass contributions of different object types. We estimated that 86% of their 42 k tonnes contribution was carried by fishing nets.

span.label: windage coefficient
span.quote: The best model fit was found for the forcing scenario with sea-surface current only (R2 = 0.52, n = 277 cells). The regression coefficient declined as we increased the atmospheric drag term (R2 = 0.39 to 0.21 depending on windage coefficient).

span.label: ghostnets
span.quote: Finally, it seems that most plastics accumulating in the GPGP region are hardly transported by winds. Our model predicted that the GPGP is dominated by objects with low or null windage coefficient, and it was the null windage forcing scenario that best represented the GPGP plastic concentrations gradients measured in this study. Furthermore, most objects captured in our trawls (e.g. broken fragments of hard plastic objects, nets and ropes) exhibited no or very little air draft when placed in seawater, and many objects sighted during the aerial expedition seemed fully submerged. Ghostnets, which were the main contributors to the total mass of GPGP plastic, generally have a draft of several metres, and therefore are unlikely to be influenced by wind transport.

span.label: Manta trawl
span.quote: After comparing plastic concentration results obtained by paired Manta and Mega net tows (n = 76 locations), we decided to use Manta and Mega trawl samples to quantify debris 0.05–5 cm and 5–50 cm in size, respectively. The comparison results and reasoning behind such decision in provided in Supplementary Methods 2.

span.label: aerial imagery
span.quote: The aerial surveys sampled a far greater area (311.0 km2) than the trawl surveys described above (3.9 km2 and 13.6 km2, for Manta and Mega net tows, respectively), thus yielding a more reliable quantification of debris larger than 50 cm, which are relatively rare.

span.label: mass concentration
span.quote: Megaplastics generally yielded the highest observed mass concentration with mean measured values of 46.3 kg km−2 (min–max: 0.4–428.1 kg km−2), followed by macroplastics with 16.8 kg km−2 (0.4–70.4 kg km−2), mesoplastics with 3.9 kg km−2 (0.0003–88.4 kg km−2), and microplastics with 2.5 kg km−2 (0.07–26.4 kg km−2). Regarding abundance however, microplastics and mesoplastics were by far the most numerous, with mean measured concentrations of 678,000 (min–max: 20,108–11,054,595) and 22,000 (261–321,712) pieces km−2 inside the GPGP against 690 (40–2,433) and 3.5 (0.5–11.6) pieces km−2 for macroplastics and megaplastics, respectively (Fig. 4b, Table 2).

span.label: numerical concentration
span.quote: Megaplastics generally yielded the highest observed mass concentration with mean measured values of 46.3 kg km−2 (min–max: 0.4–428.1 kg km−2), followed by macroplastics with 16.8 kg km−2 (0.4–70.4 kg km−2), mesoplastics with 3.9 kg km−2 (0.0003–88.4 kg km−2), and microplastics with 2.5 kg km−2 (0.07–26.4 kg km−2). Regarding abundance however, microplastics and mesoplastics were by far the most numerous, with mean measured concentrations of 678,000 (min–max: 20,108–11,054,595) and 22,000 (261–321,712) pieces km−2 inside the GPGP against 690 (40–2,433) and 3.5 (0.5–11.6) pieces km−2 for macroplastics and megaplastics, respectively (Fig. 4b, Table 2).

span.label: ENSO
span.quote: The relation between the accumulation of marine debris in the North Pacific and climate events such as El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) has previously been discussed. As such, to account for inter-annual variation, we compared latitudinal and longitudinal position of the GPGP against these two climate indexes: ENSO and PDO. We found that 2002 and 2004 were similar to the conditions experienced during our multi-vessel expedition. Thus, we compared our measurements against particle visit averages for July–September of 2002 and 2004 combined. This second attempt exhibited better results (R2 = 0.58 to 0.41, depending on forcing scenario), suggesting that climatic events such as ENSO or PDO influence the average position of the GPGP. Therefore, we decided to use the July–September average for 2002 and 2004, which better accounts for inter-annual variations in the GPGP position.

span.label: biofouling
span.quote: Buoyant plastic represents about 60% of the global plastic demand, thus nearly half of the plastic input into the oceans should sink to the floor soon after release, accumulating in sediments and underwater canyons. The rest may strand in coastlines, be ingested by marine life or removed from the sea surface due to loss of buoyancy through biofouling or aggregation.

span.label: GPGP plastic mass - MEASURED BY NET TRAWLS ALONE: about 4.8 thousand tonnes, from instruments developed to collect neustonic plankton
span.quote: Our plastic mass estimate for the GPGP (~79 k tonnes) was nearly sixteen times higher than a previous study (~4.8 k tonnes) that used net trawl data only and four times higher than another assessment (~21 k tonnes) that combined net trawl data with vessel-based visual surveys. We suggest that the increase in the estimate is mainly explained by the use of more robust methods for quantifying macro- and megaplastics over larger sea surface areas. For instance, aerial imagery allowed us to more accurately count and measure the size of sighted objects, which undeniably reduced uncertainties in mass estimates when compared to vessel-based visual surveys.

span.label: GPGP plastic mass - NET TRAWLS PLUS VESSEL SIGHTINGS: about 21 thousand tonnes, at the cost of high uncertainty in estimating a sighted object's mass
span.quote: In an attempt to overcome this misrepresentation, a research team combined net tow data with information from vessel-based visual sighting surveys. They found that while small, millimetre-sized pieces (<4.75 mm) count in trillions at global scale, they only represent a small mass portion (13%) of the total available buoyant material. Nevertheless, vessel-based sightings data yielded high uncertainties due to differences in survey protocols across research groups and difficulties in estimating the mass of sighted objects.

span.label: GPGP plastic mass - NET TRAWLS PLUS MEGA TRAWLS PLUS 311 km2 OF AERIAL IMAGERY: 79 (45-129) thousand tonnes, this study
span.quote: We predicted that the GPGP contains a total of 1.8 (mid-point estimate, low: 1.1, high: 3.6) trillion plastic pieces weighing 79 k (45 k−129 k) tonnes, comprised of debris categorised in 4 size classes: microplastics (0.05–0.5 cm), mesoplastics (0.5–5 cm), macroplastics (5–50 cm), and megaplastics (>50 cm).

span.label: what dominates the patch - BY MASS: megaplastics and macroplastics, over three quarters of it, and 86% of the megaplastic mass is fishing nets
span.quote: More than three quarters of the GPGP plastic mass was contained in the upper size classes (>5 cm), with a respective total contribution of 25% and 53% for macroplastics and megaplastics (Fig. 4a). Plastic types ‘H’ (hard plastics, sheets and films) and ‘N’ (nets, ropes and lines) represented respectively 47% and 52% of the total GPGP plastic mass, with most of micro-, meso- and macroplastic mass coming from type ‘H’, and megaplastic from type ‘N’. span.label: critiques → ocean plastic transport models integrated over several years and calibrated against datasets from different seasons and decades, which misrepresent processes that vary seasonally and inter-annually
span.quote: The relation between the accumulation of marine debris in the North Pacific and climate events such as El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) has previously been discussed. As such, to account for inter-annual variation, we compared latitudinal and longitudinal position of the GPGP against these two climate indexes: ENSO and PDO.
